difficultyReason: Five conditional answer choices with a scope shift buried in the stimulus: 'approved for clinical use' vs. 'proven safe.' Reversed-conditional trap in choice B and a too-weak distractor in choice E create high distractor density.
stimulus: A new antiviral compound has been approved for clinical use by every major regulatory agency that reviewed it. The lead researcher therefore concludes that the compound is proven safe for human consumption. Several pharmacologists dispute this conclusion. They are plainly correct to do so.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No compound that is approved for clinical use by every major regulatory agency has been adequately tested for long-term effects.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No compound that is proven safe for human consumption fails to receive approval from every major regulatory agency that reviews it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No compound is proven safe for human consumption solely on the basis of regulatory approval.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any compound that has been approved for clinical use is likely to be safe for most patients.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulatory agencies sometimes approve compounds whose long-term safety profiles are not fully understood.

explanations.correct: The conclusion to be drawn is that the pharmacologists are correct: regulatory approval does not equal proven safety. Choice C states precisely that no compound achieves 'proven safe' status solely through regulatory approval, which directly forces the inference that the researcher's move from 'approved' to 'proven safe' is illegitimate. With C, the pharmacologists' dispute follows as a matter of logic.
explanations.A: This introduces a specific empirical claim about long-term testing but does not close the logical gap between 'approved' and 'proven safe.' The conclusion is about whether approval entails proof of safety, not about what kind of testing was done.
explanations.B: This is the reversed conditional. It runs from 'proven safe' to 'approved,' not from 'approved' to 'proven safe.' It would actually lend partial support to the researcher's direction of inference, not undercut it.
explanations.D: Too weak — 'likely to be safe for most patients' is probabilistic and falls far short of the universal 'proven safe' standard needed to force the conclusion.
explanations.E: This is also too weak. 'Sometimes' does not entail that this particular compound is not proven safe; it merely raises a possibility. A sufficient assumption must force the conclusion, not merely make it plausible.

difficultyReason: The argument involves two linked conditionals in environmental law with a partial-bridge trap (choice A closes one gap but not the chain) and a near-neighbor subject-shift trap (choice D swaps 'wetlands' for 'protected habitat').
stimulus: Under the Coastal Preservation Act, any development project that displaces a protected wetland requires a mitigation permit. The proposed harbor expansion undeniably displaces a protected wetland. Nevertheless, the regional planning board has announced that no mitigation permit will be required for the project. It follows that the planning board is acting outside the scope of the Act.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any development project that requires a mitigation permit under the Act must obtain one before construction begins.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any planning board decision that conflicts with a requirement of the Coastal Preservation Act falls outside the scope of that Act.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The harbor expansion is the largest development project ever proposed in the coastal region.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any development project that displaces protected habitat of any kind falls outside the planning board's normal jurisdiction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Planning boards are rarely authorized to grant blanket exemptions to environmental regulations.

explanations.correct: The premises establish: (1) displacing a protected wetland → requires mitigation permit; (2) the harbor expansion displaces a protected wetland; therefore (3) the harbor expansion requires a mitigation permit. The board says no permit is required — this conflicts with the Act's requirement. Choice B supplies the final link: a planning board decision that conflicts with the Act's requirement falls outside the Act's scope. That forces the conclusion directly.
explanations.A: This is a partial bridge — it says a permit must be obtained before construction, which is a downstream procedural requirement. It does not connect the board's denial of the permit to acting outside the Act's scope.
explanations.C: The size of the project is entirely irrelevant to whether the Act's requirements apply or whether the board is acting within scope.
explanations.D: Subject-shift trap: 'protected habitat of any kind' is broader than 'protected wetland,' and the claim is about jurisdiction, not scope of the Act. This does not force the specific conclusion about the Act.
explanations.E: Too weak — 'rarely authorized' is probabilistic and does not establish that this board's action falls outside the Act's scope.

difficultyReason: Scope shift between 'linguistically isolated' and 'endangered' is subtle. Reversed conditional trap in choice A and a principle-wrapping trap in choice E replicate canonical Peacock-style distractor density.
stimulus: A language is considered endangered when it has fewer than one thousand fluent speakers remaining. The Koro language, spoken in the Arunachal Pradesh region of India, was documented for the first time in 2008. At the time of documentation, Koro had no more than eight hundred fluent speakers, all of whom were geographically and linguistically isolated from speakers of other languages. Some researchers have therefore claimed that Koro is not an endangered language because its speakers face no external pressure to abandon it. This claim is mistaken.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any language whose speakers are linguistically isolated from speakers of other languages is not at risk of disappearing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether a language's speakers face external pressure to abandon it has no bearing on whether that language meets the numerical threshold for endangerment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Languages with fewer than one thousand speakers can still develop robust written traditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Researchers who document a language for the first time bear special responsibility for classifying its endangerment status.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The most important factor in determining whether a language is endangered is the vitality of the cultural community that speaks it.

explanations.correct: The definition of 'endangered' given in the stimulus is purely numerical: fewer than 1,000 fluent speakers. Koro has at most 800 fluent speakers, so it meets that threshold. The researchers' claim that Koro is not endangered because speakers face no external pressure introduces a criterion not present in the stated definition. Choice B closes the gap by asserting that external pressure is irrelevant to the numerical endangerment criterion — making the researchers' rebuttal ineffective and forcing the conclusion that their claim is mistaken.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional trap: this runs from 'linguistically isolated' to 'not at risk,' which would actually support the researchers' position, not refute it.
explanations.C: Written traditions are entirely outside the scope of the argument about endangerment classification.
explanations.D: Researcher responsibility for classification is irrelevant; the argument is about what criteria determine endangerment, not who does the classifying.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap: 'most important factor' is both too vague and introduces 'cultural vitality' rather than the speaker count criterion used in the stimulus definition. It does not force the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Economic argument with a chain of three conditionals; the correct answer closes the final link while a partial-bridge trap (choice C) closes only the first two. A too-weak trap (choice D) and a subject-shift trap (choice E) complete the distractor set.
stimulus: Under the terms of the Basel Accord, any bank that holds sovereign debt rated below investment grade must maintain additional capital reserves. Meridian Bank currently holds bonds issued by a government whose debt has just been downgraded below investment grade. Meridian's chief financial officer has announced that the bank will not increase its capital reserves. It follows that Meridian Bank is now in violation of the Basel Accord.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Meridian Bank was in full compliance with the Basel Accord before the recent downgrade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Basel Accord applies to all banks that hold sovereign debt, regardless of the bank's country of incorporation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Holding sovereign debt rated below investment grade requires Meridian Bank to maintain additional capital reserves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Banks that fail to maintain required capital reserves are usually found to be in violation of the Basel Accord within one fiscal quarter.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any financial institution that does not maintain required capital reserves under an applicable accord is in violation of that accord.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any financial institution that does not maintain required capital reserves under an applicable accord is in violation of that accord.

explanations.correct: The premises establish: (1) holding below-investment-grade sovereign debt → must maintain additional capital reserves; (2) Meridian holds such debt; (3) Meridian will not increase its capital reserves. To reach 'Meridian is in violation of the Basel Accord,' we need the link: not maintaining required capital reserves → violation. Choice E supplies exactly this universal conditional, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Prior compliance is irrelevant to whether the current failure to maintain reserves constitutes a violation.
explanations.B: Jurisdiction is a distractor — the stimulus does not raise a question about whether the Accord applies to Meridian.
explanations.C: Partial-bridge trap: this restates what can already be derived from the premises (Meridian must maintain reserves) but does not connect the failure to do so to being in violation.
explanations.D: Too weak — 'usually found to be in violation within one fiscal quarter' is probabilistic and time-lagged; it does not force the conclusion that Meridian is in violation now.

difficultyReason: Ethics argument with a double scope shift: 'intends harm' vs. 'causes harm' vs. 'acts wrongly.' The correct answer bridges 'causes foreseeable harm without consent' to 'acts wrongly.' Reversed conditional trap in choice B; principle-wrapping trap in choice D.
stimulus: Dr. Arnaud administers an experimental treatment to a patient without first obtaining the patient's informed consent. The treatment ultimately causes the patient measurable physical harm. An ethics board convened to review the case concludes that Dr. Arnaud acted wrongly. A colleague argues that Dr. Arnaud cannot have acted wrongly because he did not intend to harm the patient. The ethics board's conclusion is nevertheless correct.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any physician who obtains informed consent before administering a treatment never acts wrongly in doing so.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No physician acts wrongly unless that physician causes measurable physical harm to a patient.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any physician who causes a patient measurable physical harm without that patient's informed consent has acted wrongly, regardless of the physician's intent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ethical obligations of physicians are determined primarily by the outcomes of their actions rather than by their intentions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Informed consent requirements exist to protect patients from harms they would not otherwise anticipate.

explanations.correct: The premises establish: Dr. Arnaud (i) administered treatment without informed consent and (ii) caused measurable harm. The colleague's objection is that lack of intent prevents a finding of wrongdoing. Choice C states that causing measurable harm without informed consent constitutes acting wrongly regardless of intent — this directly defeats the colleague's objection and forces the ethics board's conclusion.
explanations.A: This addresses physicians who do obtain consent — the opposite of Dr. Arnaud's situation. It is irrelevant to whether Dr. Arnaud acted wrongly.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap: this says harm is necessary for wrongdoing, but the question is whether the combination of harm + no consent is sufficient for wrongdoing. Choice B would actually help the colleague's argument by focusing on harm in isolation.
explanations.D: Principle-wrapping trap: 'determined primarily by outcomes' is too vague and does not universally entail that this specific act was wrong — it still allows that intent could be a secondary factor sufficient to excuse conduct.
explanations.E: This gives a rationale for informed consent rules but does not establish that violating them plus causing harm equals acting wrongly. It does not force the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Technology/policy argument where the scope shift between 'open-source' and 'publicly auditable' is subtle. Partial-bridge trap in choice A and a near-neighbor subject-shift trap in choice D ('government software' vs. 'voting software') create high distractor density.
stimulus: Critics of electronic voting systems argue that any voting software whose source code is not publicly auditable poses an unacceptable risk to electoral integrity. The software currently used in Heron County's elections is proprietary, and its source code has never been made available for public review. One county commissioner argues that since the software was certified by a federally accredited testing laboratory, the critics' concern does not apply to Heron County's system.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion that the commissioner's argument is flawed to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Federally accredited testing laboratories do not always examine the full source code of the software they certify.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Federal certification of voting software does not make that software's source code publicly auditable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any voting software that has been certified by a federally accredited laboratory has met at least minimum federal security standards.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any government software that is not publicly auditable should be replaced with open-source alternatives as soon as practicable.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proprietary software vendors have a financial interest in preventing public scrutiny of their source code.

explanations.correct: The critics' standard is 'publicly auditable source code.' The commissioner argues that federal certification answers the critics' concern. For the commissioner's argument to be flawed, federal certification must not satisfy the 'publicly auditable' criterion. Choice B states exactly this: federal certification does not make source code publicly auditable. With B, the certified-but-not-auditable Heron County software still meets the critics' problematic description, and the commissioner's rebuttal collapses.
explanations.A: Partial-bridge trap: even if labs don't always examine full source code, it's possible they did in this case. This weakens the commissioner's argument probabilistically but does not force the conclusion that the argument is flawed.
explanations.C: This supports the commissioner's position rather than undermining it — it affirms that certification means something.
explanations.D: Subject-shift trap: 'government software' is broader than 'voting software,' and the prescription to replace software is outside the scope of the argument about the commissioner's reasoning.
explanations.E: Financial interest is a motive-questioning distractor that does not logically connect certification to public auditability.

difficultyReason: History argument with a triple conditional chain. The correct answer closes the final link (from 'distorted the historical record' to 'should be revised'). A too-weak trap uses 'often' and a reversed conditional trap runs the key link backwards.
stimulus: Historians generally agree that any official account of a war that omits documented atrocities committed by the victorious side has distorted the historical record. The account of the Tamberlaine Campaign published in the Veldoran National Archives omits documented atrocities committed by Veldo's forces, which ultimately prevailed. The Veldoran Historical Society has argued that the Archives' account should not be revised because it was compiled by the leading scholars of the era. Their argument is unconvincing.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any official historical account that has distorted the record should be revised, regardless of the scholarly credentials of its authors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No official historical account compiled by leading scholars of its era has ever been found to contain factual errors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any official account that should be revised will eventually be corrected by subsequent generations of historians.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historical accounts that omit atrocities often reflect the political priorities of the governments that commissioned them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An official account should be revised only if the scholars who compiled it are no longer alive to defend their methodology.

explanations.correct: The premises establish: (1) omitting documented atrocities by the victorious side → distorted the historical record; (2) the Archives' account omits such atrocities; therefore (3) the Archives' account has distorted the record. To conclude the Society's argument is unconvincing, we need: distorted record → should be revised, regardless of author credentials. Choice A supplies exactly this, neutralizing the Society's scholarly-credentials defense and forcing the conclusion.
explanations.B: This is irrelevant and, if anything, contradicts the premises — it implies leading scholars don't make errors, which would support the Society's position.
explanations.C: That revision will eventually happen does not address whether the Society's argument against revision is unconvincing now.
explanations.D: Too weak — 'often reflect political priorities' is probabilistic and does not force the conclusion that this account should be revised.
explanations.E: Reversed conditional trap: this would make scholarly credentials a sufficient condition to block revision (revise only if authors are deceased), which supports the Society's argument rather than defeating it.

difficultyReason: Policy/environmental argument. The scope shift between 'carbon-neutral' and 'environmentally sustainable' is the core trap. Reversed conditional in choice C; principle-wrapping in choice E; subject-shift in choice D ('renewable energy projects' vs. 'biofuel projects').
stimulus: A proposed biofuel production facility in the Mireille Valley would be powered entirely by solar energy, making its operations carbon-neutral. Proponents argue that the facility therefore qualifies as an environmentally sustainable project under the Regional Development Plan. Critics contend that the facility would drain a nearby aquifer at a rate that cannot be naturally replenished. The proponents' argument should be rejected.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No project that irreversibly depletes a natural resource is environmentally sustainable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No carbon-neutral project has ever been approved under the Regional Development Plan without extensive environmental review.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any environmentally sustainable project must be powered exclusively by solar or wind energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any renewable energy project that depletes groundwater resources should be subject to heightened regulatory scrutiny.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Environmental sustainability requires that a project's total ecological impact, not merely its carbon profile, be assessed holistically.

explanations.correct: The critics establish that the facility would drain an aquifer at an unreplenishable rate — i.e., it irreversibly depletes a natural resource. Choice A states that no such project is environmentally sustainable. Combined with the critics' factual claim, this forces the conclusion that the facility is not environmentally sustainable, meaning the proponents' argument (carbon-neutral → environmentally sustainable) should be rejected.
explanations.B: Procedural history of approvals under the Plan is irrelevant to whether the facility qualifies as environmentally sustainable.
explanations.C: Reversed conditional trap: this runs from 'environmentally sustainable' to 'solar or wind powered,' whereas the argument runs the other direction. It also concerns power source alone, not aquifer depletion.
explanations.D: Subject-shift trap: 'renewable energy projects' is broader than biofuel projects specifically, and 'heightened scrutiny' is a procedural remedy that does not force the conclusion that the proponents' argument should be rejected.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap: 'holistic assessment' is an intuitive but vague standard. It does not specifically entail that aquifer depletion disqualifies a project, so it does not force the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Arts/criticism argument mirroring Peacock/Hacker structure: a critic's categorical claim about artistic form is challenged via a counterexample, requiring a linking premise about what constitutes the relevant property. Reversed conditional in choice D; principle-wrapping in choice E.
stimulus: Several influential critics have asserted that any novel structured as a non-linear, fragmented narrative is aesthetically uncommitted — unable to take a definitive moral stance. This is demonstrably wrong. Consider Elena Ferrante's Neapolitan novels and W.G. Sebald's The Rings of Saturn: both employ non-linear, fragmented narrative structures and yet both take unmistakably clear and forceful moral positions throughout.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No novelist who employs a non-linear narrative structure is capable of writing a morally committed work of fiction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Neapolitan novels and The Rings of Saturn are among the most commercially successful novels of the past three decades.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No novel that takes unmistakably clear and forceful moral positions throughout is aesthetically uncommitted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any novel that is aesthetically uncommitted relies on fragmented narrative structure to conceal its lack of moral stance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The moral seriousness of a novel is best measured by the directness and clarity of its narrative voice rather than by its structural choices.

explanations.correct: The counterexample establishes that Ferrante's and Sebald's novels take unmistakably clear and forceful moral positions. To refute the critics' claim that non-linear fragmented novels are 'aesthetically uncommitted,' we need the bridge: novels with clear and forceful moral positions are not aesthetically uncommitted. Choice C supplies exactly this universal negative, forcing the conclusion that the critics are wrong.
explanations.A: This endorses the critics' view rather than refuting it — it restates their categorical claim. Adding this premise makes the critics correct, not wrong.
explanations.B: Commercial success is entirely irrelevant to the argument about moral commitment in narrative structure.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap: this runs from 'aesthetically uncommitted' to 'fragmented narrative,' the opposite direction of the critics' claim. It does not connect 'clear moral positions' to 'not aesthetically uncommitted.'
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap: 'best measured by narrative voice' is an interpretive principle that does not universally entail that these specific novels are not aesthetically uncommitted. It is too indeterminate to force the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Policy/economics argument where 'price controls' vs. 'market distortions' vs. 'long-run supply reduction' form a three-step chain. Partial-bridge trap in choice B; too-weak trap in choice C; reversed conditional in choice E.
stimulus: Economists who study rental markets have established that any rent-control ordinance that caps prices below the market-clearing level creates a market distortion. The city of Vanthorpe has enacted a rent-control ordinance that caps apartment rents at fifty percent of current market rates. Several city council members have argued that this ordinance will increase housing availability for low-income residents. This argument fails to account for the ordinance's full consequences.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any ordinance that caps prices below the market-clearing level will eventually be challenged in court by affected landlords.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Vanthorpe ordinance caps apartment rents below the market-clearing level and therefore creates a market distortion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rent-control ordinances sometimes discourage new construction and can reduce housing supply over time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any market distortion in a rental market reduces the long-run supply of available housing units, thereby harming the residents the ordinance was intended to benefit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any policy that reduces long-run housing supply is one that creates a market distortion in the rental sector.

explanations.correct: The premises establish a chain: rent-control below market-clearing → market distortion; the Vanthorpe ordinance caps at 50% of market rates (below market-clearing) → market distortion. To conclude the council members' argument 'fails to account for the ordinance's full consequences,' we need the final link: market distortion → reduces long-run housing supply → harms intended beneficiaries. Choice D supplies this complete final link, forcing the conclusion that the council members have overlooked a harmful downstream consequence.
explanations.A: Legal challenge by landlords is a procedural distractor entirely outside the scope of the argument about housing availability and market consequences.
explanations.B: Partial-bridge trap: this restates a conclusion already derivable from the premises (the ordinance creates a distortion) but does not connect the distortion to reduced housing supply or to the council members' argument being incomplete.
explanations.C: Too weak — 'sometimes discourage' and 'can reduce' are probabilistic hedges that do not force the conclusion. A sufficient assumption must eliminate uncertainty about whether the harmful consequence follows.
explanations.E: Reversed conditional trap: this runs from 'reduces long-run housing supply' to 'creates a market distortion,' the opposite direction of what is needed. We already have distortion established; what is missing is the link forward from distortion to supply reduction.
